title: Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining EU
description: Turbulent international affairs have brought the vote forward, but the campaign has focused more on Iceland's vital fishing industry.
fullText:
Icelanders are voting in a referendum to decide whether to resume talks on joining the European Union, 13 years after they were broken off.

In an indication of how tight the result is expected to be, the latest opinion poll put the No campaign in the lead with 51.6%. An earlier poll had put the Yes campaign ahead.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government had already intended to hold a referendum, but turbulent international affairs prompted her to bring it forward.

But the debate was fought less over Nato member Iceland's security concerns than over its vital fishing industry and sovereignty.

Iceland has a population of under 400,000. More than one in five voters had already cast their ballots in early voting before Saturday, according to Iceland's public broadcaster RUV.

The question on the ballot is: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

Although Iceland is already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone as part of the European Economic Area, EU membership would bring it into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland's application to join the EU was already well advanced when it put talks on hold in 2013, and European Commission officials have indicated that talks could be finalised in one or two years. Of the 35 so-called chapters of talks ranging from fisheries and economic policy to freedom of speech and free movement of goods, 27 had begun and 11 of them were provisionally complete.

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU. It would mean backing a move towards an accession agreement. Any deal would then have to be approved by a second referendum, as well by parliament, and the constitution would have to be amended. The EU's 27 member states would also have to sign it off.

One Yes-campaign group, "Yes to See", says Icelanders should at least see what deal they can get, so they have all the information before a final decision.

Equally, a No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.

Sovereignty has been a crucial issue in the pre-referendum debate. Iceland fought hard to become fully independent from Denmark in 1944, and its fishing and marine industries make up almost 40% of exports.

The No campaign fears losing control over Iceland's prized fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and has vowed never to share the country's waters with anyone. Brussels has indicated Iceland could earn some kind of exemption, but it is considered potentially the biggest obstacle to any agreement.

Many Icelanders remember the so-called Cod Wars with the UK that Iceland won in the 1970s. And fisheries was always the issue that stopped Iceland joining the EU before.

However, in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system, Reykjavik moved to start accession talks in 2009, only to bring them to a halt in 2013.

Iceland is now one of Europe's most affluent nations and Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC that "many people attribute this to Iceland's independence".

One Icelandic trade union survey suggested this year that the country was the most expensive in the world, far pricier than its Nordic neighbours.

Although it has the fifth highest GDP (economic output) per capita in the world, interest rates are stubbornly high at 8% and inflation has climbed to 5.6%.

Yes campaigners argue that the economic benefits of the EU would help bring the rates down.

Iceland may be a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

A bilateral US defence agreement has been in place since 1951 and the No campaign has said Iceland's security rests on both Nato and the US, and that EU membership is not a substitute for Nato.

Iceland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have viewed Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island with alarm.

However, there has also been concern at US President Donald Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland - especially the fact that he has confused it with Iceland.

This year the EU and Iceland signed a security and defence partnership, and EU officials said the EU "offers an anchor in a community of values, prosperity and security".

Ahead of the referendum, the two sides held a televised debate where the Yes campaign team was headed by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir and the No campaign was led by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, chair of the opposition Independence Party.

Kristrún told the audience that Iceland was already well integrated in the European Union, and becoming a member would be "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take".

She also made clear that a Yes vote did not necessarily mean that Iceland would join, and that if there was a No vote, the result would be respected.

Guðrún, meanwhile, stressed that the vote was not about whether Iceland should work well with Europe: "We already do, and we want that to continue."

Instead, she portrayed the referendum as a vote on whether Icelanders wanted to hand "decision-making powers" to Brussels on fisheries, agriculture and their natural resources.

Although geopolitics kick-started the government's decision to push for a return to EU talks, there has been little discussion of it during the campaign.

"It's lower on the agenda than many would think," says Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

title: Toolchestrator – make local, AI-built tools usable by your team
description: You vibe-coded it. Toolchestrator runs it for the whole team, and for your AI. No migration, no rewrite; your apps stay on the machine you built them on.
fullText:
The part that makes it infrastructure, not a dashboard. Connect the hub to Claude, or any MCP client, and your AI discovers your team's tools, reads their shared data, and runs their actions, with exactly your permissions. Set it up in a minute.

Every connected tool announces what it is, who built it, and which problem it solves, so the next person searches before they rebuild.

Leave a note on a tool, or pin one to a specific data model: how to run it, what not to touch on a Friday, the gotcha that cost someone an afternoon. Team knowledge that lives next to the tool, not lost in chat.

Tools publish the records worth sharing. Teammates and other tools read them with filters (“open invoices over €1,000”) straight from the hub, even when the source machine is asleep.

Every tool lists the actions it can perform. Pick one, press Run, see the result, executed on the owner's machine and delivered to your screen.

If a tool has a web interface, teammates open it with one click and use it as if it ran on their own machine. A floating switcher hops between your team's apps.

Built a TUI or an interactive command-line tool? Serve it through the hub and a teammate drives it live in their browser, keystrokes and all. The program still runs on your machine, and only the screen travels.

A live picture of your tool ecosystem: which tools feed which, who reads what and why. Drawn from real usage, not wishful documentation.

When one tool's data feeds another, those fields become a contract. If an AI edit would remove or change one, it's flagged with exactly which teammate's tool breaks, before it happens.
 amount · read by Reorder Planner

Chain tools into multi-step flows, or let one tool react the moment another's data changes. Orchestration without scheduled scripts to babysit.

Machines sleep. Work queues. When a tool comes back online it picks up whatever was asked of it, and everyone can see, live, what's reachable right now.

Every tool starts private. Its owner decides: keep it personal, share with a department, or open it to the company. One switch governs the data, the actions, and the app.

title: Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver
description: How to give a coding agent a real world, real demand, a protected measure, and enough memory to improve a complex feature.
fullText:
The first agent loops we built were barely loops: give the agent a plan, let it work until the tests pass, and return failures. That works when the tests describe the job. It fails when the job is to grow a product capability that we do not understand yet.

The agent keeps moving, but movement is not the problem. The tests only protect what we already know, and the important failures sit outside them. A screen can look complete while it stores nothing. An agent can give the right answer for the wrong reason. A scorer can reward behavior no user wants. More turns make each of those failures cheaper and faster.

In The Convergence Problem I argued that agents can own turns while people own rounds. I did not describe what the agent needs between those boundaries. It needs a harness that does three things. The harness must expose a real failure, locate the missing capability, and preserve the lesson after the session ends. That is a different machine from an agent with a retry prompt.

The obvious system is the feature. The less obvious one is the process that decides what the agent should change next. We have to engineer both.

The development agent changes the feature. The driver approaches the feature through the same surface a user would. The scorer reads what happened. The controller then chooses the next gap from that evidence. Repository state carries the decision into the next session.

An agent product usually puts another agent inside the feature. The two agents must remain separate. The development agent knows the code and the expected result. The product agent gets a fresh conversation and only the tools that the product exposes.

If they share context, the test is worthless. The product agent can succeed with knowledge that a user will never provide. The same harness works without a product agent. The driver can use a browser, API, command, or hardware simulator.

The prompt gets most of the attention because it is easy to see. The loop depends more on the world around it. First, the harness needs a reproducible starting point. The data, services, model, environment, and served code must match the recorded run. A reset should return the system to that point. A preflight should prove that it did.

If the world is unhealthy, the harness records no score. Infrastructure trouble is not evidence that the feature failed. This distinction prevents a large class of false repairs. Missing data can look like weak reasoning. Stale code can look like a broken contract.

Next, the harness needs real demand. We use a small corpus of requests that a person wrote or approved. The driver sends one request unchanged through a fresh interaction. It records the answer, tool calls, rejected actions, visible result, and persistent effects.

The effects matter most. Software can describe the correct action without performing it. It can render a plausible screen without changing the system beneath it. The prompt is therefore only one input to the run. The fixture, code revision, model, contract, and scorer belong beside it. A score without those inputs is only a number.

Every loop needs a deterministic floor. Tests, validators, schemas, and effect checks hold behavior that the feature already earned. The floor starts green. If it turns red, that regression becomes the next job. The floor cannot tell us what to build next. For that, we drive a real request and inspect the shortfall.

Some shortfalls support a mechanical score. Others need a screenshot, repeated samples, or a person who understands the work. Those signals can be noisy. One perfect run proves that success is possible. It says little about whether success is reliable.

The signals choose a direction, while the floor preserves prior progress. That separation keeps the loop honest. A new capability can move the product forward without erasing the path behind it.

Once the world and measures exist, the round itself is simple.

One gap does not mean one file. It means one causal claim. The missing capability may cross the data model, tool contract, runtime, agent instruction, interface, and effect check. The round should close that whole path.

Partial paths create the most convincing failures. The interface exists, but nothing produces its data. The tool returns success, but the state does not change. A narrow path that works from request to effect is worth more than five layers of unfinished possibility.

The classification step prevents random repairs. A symptom can belong to the world, domain, contract, runtime, steering, surface, or harness. Without that step, every agent failure becomes a prompt problem. Every visual failure becomes a frontend problem. The loop changes the nearest thing instead of the right thing.

Changing one causal gap also makes the result attributable. If a round changes five independent levers, nobody knows which lesson to preserve.

An autonomous loop will optimize whatever measure it can reach, including a bad one. The harness therefore needs an authority model. Ours has three levels.

Free files are normal implementation levers. The loop can change and measure them inside the assigned scope. Propose files cross a boundary. The loop can record evidence and suggest a change, but a person decides. Frozen files define the exam. They include the approved corpus, fixture, existing rungs, score rules, and judgment rubric.

The loop can add a regression check for a failure it observed. It cannot weaken an existing check or lower the threshold. It also cannot change a product lever and the measure of that lever in the same round. Otherwise, it grades its own repair.

Learned judges need the same protection. A visual judge remains evidence until its rankings agree with repeated human rankings. This limits the loop’s authority, but it makes the result credible.

Every product round also tests the harness. The driver can hide a failure. The fixture can omit a necessary case. The scorer can punish correct behavior. The procedure can waste the same hour twice.

We end each round with one question:

What cost time that a rule or check could prevent?

The first occurrence becomes evidence. Repeated friction can change the driver, facts, or standing procedure. Self-improvement happens when the loop promotes a specific failure into a durable constraint. It does not rewrite its operating system after every surprise. Sometimes the right change is subtraction. A false warning or misleading rung teaches the loop to avoid good behavior.

There are really three loops running at different speeds. The product loop closes one capability each round. The harness loop changes when repeated evidence exposes a development failure. The direction loop sits outside both. A person reads a batch of evidence and decides whether to continue, redirect, or stop.

Keeping those loops separate matters. The development agent can propose a new direction. It cannot decide that its own result is good enough.

None of this can live only in the current conversation. Agent sessions end, context compresses, and the next session starts without the old reasoning. We keep a small package under goals/:

LOOP.md changes when the process changes. STATE.md changes after each round. The distinction makes sessions disposable without making the work forgetful. A new agent reads the goal, procedure, state, and evidence, then continues from the same decision.

This is more than context preservation. The files make the development process inspectable. We can see why the loop chose a gap, which evidence supported the change, and whether the next run improved the same request.

We run the inner loop in small batches. Three rounds usually produce enough evidence for a decision without giving the system room to drift. At the boundary, a person chooses whether to continue the queue, redirect the next batch, or stop. The loop stops sooner when it cannot reproduce or attribute a failure. It also stops when the world is unhealthy or the repair needs a frozen change.

This is the human-owned round from the convergence post. The agent owns the turns inside it. The boundary exists because the score cannot decide the product’s direction.

Most tickets do not need any of this. If complete tests describe the work, give the agent the tests and let it finish. The harness earns its cost when use must reveal the capability sequence. The system must also expose effects that the harness can observe.

Start with three requests, one fixture, one score command, one loop file, one state file, and a three-round budget. Add a new control only after a failure justifies it.

The quality of an agent loop is not how long it runs or how many commits it produces. It is what remains after a round. A good round leaves a working capability, evidence that it works, and a harness that will not pay for the same lesson twice. That is an agent loop worth leaving alone with a complex feature.

title: 'Small steps' for Schmidt at Ulster - Best
description: Rory Best says Joe Schmidt's new role with Ulster is a case of "small steps" as the province seek to use the former Ireland coach's expertise to build a platform for long-term success.
fullText:
Rory Best says Joe Schmidt's new role with Ulster is a case of "small steps" as the province seek to use the former Ireland coach's expertise to build a platform for long-term success.

Schmidt was appointed Ulster's coach development adviser last month after ending his two-year stint as Australia boss, a newly created role focused on the province's coaching pathway.

The 60-year-old is one of Ireland's most successful coaches having led the national team to three Six Nations titles - including the 2018 Grand Slam - during a six-year spell and Leinster to two European Cups.

"I don't want to just be successful this season or in a year or two, it has to be a continuous process and to do that we need continuity of what's coming behind it and that's why Joe is here," said Ulster general manager Rory Best, who was appointed Ireland captain by Schmidt in 2016.

"Joe was the best coach I worked under as a head coach. Since then, he's went on, he's coached the All Blacks, Australia. He's across the New Zealand underage system, the Australian underage system, from his time in Leinster the Irish underage system.

"So to bring all the best practices together, ultimately what you want to do is to create a conveyor belt. The lift it gives everyone around the place is brilliant. We're delighted to have him.

"Obviously the next step is to get him head to toe in Ulster gear, but it's small steps."

Schmidt was present at an open training session for Ulster's senior men's team in Banbridge on Friday as Murphy's side ramp up preparations for the 2026-27 season.

Murphy - who worked alongside the Kiwi at Leinster and Ireland - said it was a "genius idea" by Best to get Schmidt involved.

"Myself and Joe go back a long time. Besty, I thought it was a genius idea bringing him over," he said.

"He's helping through the pathway and having a look at that area and making sure we have a supply of players to feed this Ulster senior team.

"He's here today to have a look at training and we'd be crazy not to use a person like that in relation in giving us a bit of feedback about how we go about our business."

Murphy is in the process of reintegrating Ulster's cohort of Ireland internationals back into training after their Nations Championship exertions in July.

A promising 2025-26 season ended in disappointing fashion for Ulster as they missed out on Investec Champions Cup qualification after finishing ninth in the United Rugby Championship and losing the Challenge Cup final to Montpellier.

Ulster face Edinburgh and Ospreys in pre-season friendlies before beginning their URC campaign against the former in Belfast on 25 September.

During a busy summer of squad additions and departures, Ulster signed the likes of forwards Eli Snyman, Ben Donnell and Keynan Knox and backs Chay Mullins, Matthew Devine and Jamie Benson, while losing key players such as Werner Kok and Angus Bell.

"I think our squad depth has improved, especially in key positions," said Murphy, who is entering his third full season in charge.

"Ben Donnell can play in back row and second row, Eli in the second row gives us more experience in that area. Two tight-heads knocking around in Keynan Knox and Eduardo Bello creates pressure and competition for places which is really positive.

"Tom O'Toole, Scotty Wilson and Tom McAllister were there last year, those lads have to fight it out now to get themselves on the pitch, which is great.

"Our two half-backs that have come in, Matty Devine and young Benson, they've both fitted in really well and upped the level of competition to get your name on the sheet, so that's been really positive."

title: Pritchard retains rowing world title in Amsterdam
description: Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard retains his PR1 men's single sculls world title at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam.
fullText:
Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard retained his PR1 men's single sculls world title at the Rowing World Championships in Amsterdam.

Pritchard, from Mumbles near Swansea, crossed the line in eight minutes and 50.46 seconds to set a new record at the World Championships.

The 34-year-old finished just shy of the eight minutes and 40.38 seconds world record time he set at the 2025 European Championships in Plovdiv, Bulgaria.

After a strong start, Italian Giacomo Perini and Australian Erik Horrie closed the gap on Pritchard towards the 500m mark before the Welshman stretched his lead, eventually winning by 6.81 seconds.

Pritchard named BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year 2025

Pritchard is one of para-rowing's leading forces. Since winning Paralympic gold in 2024, he has set multiple world records and added European and world titles to his list of accolades.

The 2025 BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year award winner and his rivals had to deal with adversity during the championships in the Netherlands, with their semi-final delayed due to thunderstorms, reducing recovery windows.

Pritchard's second world championship win came weeks after claiming the 2026 European title in Varese, Italy, and having suffered an injury earlier this month.

After retaining his global title, Pritchard told World Rowing it had been a "story of calamities" following Friday's thunderstorms and the issues he faced in the race.

He also noted his rivals are "getting faster off the first 500".

Pritchard added: "But you've just got to try and back yourself, back all the training that you do.

"We're in some lovely Welsh weather at the moment, some liquid sunshine, so it's great that all the training that I do on the (river) Tawe back home."

title: Hospitalised Goodwin to miss Dundee United's Kilmarnock trip
description: Jim Goodwin will be missing from Dundee United's dugout against Kilmarnock on Saturday after taking ill and being admitted to hospital on Thursday, the Scottish Premiership club confirm.
fullText:
Jim Goodwin will be missing from Dundee United's dugout against Kilmarnock on Saturday after taking ill and being admitted to hospital on Thursday, the Scottish Premiership club have confirmed.

Assistant Lee Sharp took first-team training at United's St Andrews base on Friday and also assumed pre-match media duties in 44-year-old Goodwin's absence.

He could not say at the time whether the Irishman would return for the trip to Rugby Park.

But the club have now stated on X: "Dundee United manager Jim Goodwin will not be in attendance at today's fixture versus Kilmarnock as he continues to deal with an ongoing medical matter.

"The manager would like to thank everyone for their kind wishes and comments over the last 24 hours.

"The club would ask that his privacy, and that of his family, is respected at this time.

"We do not intend to provide any further medical detail and will issue an update when appropriate."

United have one point after three Premiership matches, while Saturday's opponents are yet to register a point this term after two games.

Sharp had said on Friday: "He is OK. I spoke to him last night and I spoke to him again this morning and he was in good spirits.

title: Trippier praises Miley's 'big presence' as Newcastle face Tonali reunion
description: Newcastle midfielder Lewis Miley is backed to "go as far as he wants" as the 20-year-old prepares to face former team-mate Sandro Tonali at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
fullText:
It has been an eventful summer on Tyneside, but 25 May proved a particularly significant date.

On the same day Tottenham Hotspur manager Roberto de Zerbi reached out to Sandro Tonali, Newcastle United announced Lewis Miley had signed a new long-term contract.

Newcastle have recruited three midfielders this summer to offset the departures of Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes to Spurs and Arsenal, but it is rather telling that manager Matthias Jaissle is already a "big fan" of one he inherited.

Jaissle certainly did not think twice about starting Miley against Liverpool on the opening weekend, despite him only playing 45 minutes in pre-season following a spell out with a broken leg.

Newcastle have since signed Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City in a deal worth up to £52m,, external but the new arrival is expected to complement Miley rather than hinder his progress and the academy graduate looks set to keep his place as he faces Tonali for the first time at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday (17:30 BST).

After previously learning from Tonali and Guimaraes, the 20-year-old now has the chance to step up in his natural role in the middle of the park.

Kieran Trippier believes his "very humble" former team-mate Miley is "more than capable" of doing just that.

"You can see the development from when he first started training with the first team to where he is now," the ex-England defender said.

"He's become a big presence and his ability for his age is immense. He can go as far as he wants to - I believe in him that much.

"But the most important thing is that he's grounded and always wants to learn. That will stand him in really good stead."

Miley's level-headedness also made him a firm favourite of former Newcastle head coach Eddie Howe.

Howe even trusted Miley to fill in out of postion at right-back when Tino Livramento sustained a series of niggling injuries in his final campaign in charge.

Miley, as a result, ended up playing the most minutes (1,403) of any English teenager in the Premier League last season before he turned 20 in May.

Of those players aged 19 and under in the top flight at the time, from all nations, Miley ranked first for assists (four), successful passes (738), successful passes in the final third (188) and line-breaking passes (164).

But he also showed the gritty side of his game.

Although Miley played a number of matches at full-back, which naturally led to more defensive situations, he was still first among teenagers for interceptions (20), second for possession won (69) and third for successful duels (84).

He has since taken that experience back into midfield and put in an assured all-round performance in the 2-2 draw against Liverpool last week.

"Not to put too much pressure on him but, honestly, coming back from a long injury with a really short pre-season and showing that in the first match is something special," Jaissle said.

"I'm just proud to be a part of his development now because, hopefully, we have a player with a really bright future."

No wonder Jaissle gave Miley a bear hug after he came off.

Jaissle is keen not to burden Miley, whose younger brother Mason is also on the club's books, but he has cautiously namechecked the midfielder as someone who could potentially take on additional responsibility in the years to come.

Not least after those who departed this summer left a "vacuum" in the German's own words.

While Miley is not necessarily a vocal figure, it has felt he has been building up to a more prominent role in the side in his own calm, understated way.

Trippier even handed the boyhood Newcastle supporter the captain's armband against PSV in the Champions League last season, which felt like a passing of the torch.

"He deserved that moment, to captain his club in the Champions League at the age he was," Trippier said.

"It must have been an amazing feeling for him and I couldn't have been happier for him. He's definitely got the qualities to step up and become a leader in his own way."

title: Itauma v Hrgovic - heavyweight world title fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight world title fight between Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic.
fullText:
Britain could have a new heavyweight world champion on Saturday when Moses Itauma faces Croatian Filip Hrgovic at London's O2 Arena for the vacant IBF title.

The 21-year-old Briton has won all 14 of his professional fights, 12 by stoppage, and has established himself as one of the division's most exciting young prospects.

A victory would make the Chatham fighter the youngest heavyweight world champion since Mike Tyson in 1986.

But Hrgovic is a major step up. The experienced 34-year-old - a 2016 Olympic bronze medallist - has a record of 20 wins and one defeat, with 15 victories inside the distance.

You can follow radio commentary from 21:00 BST on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, before switching to BBC Radio 5 Live from 22:00.

Live text commentary will begin at 19:30 on the BBC Sport website and app.

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for the bout.

"Hrgovic right now is possibly the best fighter for him to face. On paper it's a test but I don't think it will be a test. I don't think Moses will be under any form of pressure in a fight like this.

"I think it's going to be one of Moses' easiest nights of his career and he'll win a world title."

"I do have Itauma as the favourite. He is no doubt a better fighter but still unproven over the long distance. And think people are maybe just forgetting just how tough Hrgovic is and how good he is at taking a shot.

"I can see Itauma blowing him away early because he's so accurate but I can also see Hrgovic riding the storm and it becoming a more difficult fight in the second half for Itauma.

"But I still see Moses coming out on top. Hrgovic cuts a lot and I can see this being stopped on cuts because Itauma will hit him so often."

"It's a really good fight. It's a test that Itauma has been needing for a while. Stylistically, it's very interesting. I think this fight will be really hard or really easy. I don't see a middle ground where Itauma will cruise and will look great doing it.

"I think he either gets rid of him inside three rounds or this is the acid test we've all been waiting for.

"Hrgovic is brave and tough but he stands up tall and is quite easy to hit. Itauma has got the whole package. He's in and out of range, he's sharp. He's got the footwork and speed of a cruiserweight and the power of a heavyweight.

"So I'll go with Itauma inside three rounds."

"I've said for a while that I'd back Moses againt any heavyweight on the planet, other than Oleksandr Usyk. Going by Usyk's last performance against Rico Verhoeven, I'd probably back Moses against him too.

"Hrgovic is technically good and will ask Itauma a few more questions than previous opponents. But ultimately, I think the speed and timing of Moses will be the difference.

"He will get to him in the sixth or seventh round and stop him, with maybe a few knockdowns along the way."

"I favour Moses to get the win. I know Hrgovic will come prepared. He's game and not a pushover. He's coming to win a world title. So it won't be a straightforward fight, but it will be a good fight.

"I'm rooting for Moses so I say he will win by any means necessary. Whether it's points, stoppage or even a disqualification."

"I fancy Itauma to make a statement with a stoppage mid to late rounds. I think the cuts of Hrgovic may come into play, but I also think Itauma will take his time, find the gaps and then get the stoppage."

"Both men can punch hard - expect fireworks on Saturday. This is the acid test for Itauma. You have to favour the younger man because of his southpaw speed, skill, IQ and the foundations seem to be there for a huge career ahead.

"But Hrgovic has momentum and this is his chance for a world title and he will leave no stone unturned."

"I think it's Itauma's time and he stops him. I think he will be too much for a 34-year-old Hrgovic, who has never really pushed on like we expected him to.

"It could be with sharp punches and he knocks Hrgovic out within four or five rounds, or he stops him on cuts a little bit later on. Hrgovic's skin really shreds and that's the danger with Itauma's punches. His timing and accuracy is really good.

"Hrgovic is very tough, but he can be one dimensional in terms of his feet coming forward. He's a bit cumbersome and he leans back and is there to be hit.

"I think Itauma will close the distance really well going forward or dropping back with great devastating counter-punches as he's retreating."

"As this fight gets closer - and this always happens with big fights - opinions change. My opinion hasn't changed but it has definitely got tighter.

"I still think Itauma will get this done but I'm not as convinced as I was three or four months ago. Hrgovic looks in incredible shape. He's been training away in the mountains of Big Bear Lake in California with Abel Sanchez.

"I do think Itauma gets it done between rounds six and eight and it's a stoppage on cuts, but not without facing some trouble first."

"This is, on paper, a test for Itauma. Hrgovic is big, strong and his resume is far stronger.

"But still, are we allowed to dream about a young heavyweight who could change the landscape? I think we should.

"Itauma has the speed, agility, and the thought process of his work is what sets him apart from other heavyweights right now.

"I really strongly believe he will do a job on Saturday. I think he will be impressive and wear down a really robust and physically tough Hrgovic.

"I think Itauma wins within six rounds."

title: Beaugrand wins again in Weihai as Potter second
description: France's Cassandre Beaugrand earns her fourth straight win in the World Triathlon Championship Series as Britain's Beth Potter comes second in Weihai.
fullText:
France's Cassandre Beaugrand earned her fourth straight win in the World Triathlon Championship Series as Britain's Beth Potter came second in Weihai.

Olympic champion Beaugrand surged away in the final kilometre of the 10km run to finish in one minute 49.20 seconds and maintain her perfect record in this season's Championship Series.

Beaugrand's victory in China followed a thrilling tussle up until the final stretch, as Olympic bronze medalist Potter finished six seconds behind the 29-year-old.

Germany's Lisa Tertsch was third, a further 18 seconds back.

"This one was definitely not easy," said Beaugrand.

"I was feeling great on the swim, great on the bike. The run was quite hard with Beth pushing the pace. I just tried my best to keep up and trust my finish."

Beaugrand exited the two-lap 1500m swim in third behind Britain's Tilly Anema and Brazil's Vittoria Lopez.

After a close bike section, where a pack of more than 30 cyclists merged together at the front, Beaugrand, Potter and Tertsch started to break away on foot.

On the final lap as Tertsch started to fade away, Potter fought valiantly but she could not keep in touch with Beaugrand's searing pace.

Beaugrand's victory means she has overtaken Potter, despite competing in fewer races this year, to go top of the World Triathlon Championship Series standings.

The men's race was won by Switzerland's Max Studer, who finished in 1:41:08.

Spain's David Cantero del Campo finished 10 seconds behind, with Canada's Tyler Mislawchuk in third, a further seven seconds back.

There is one more regular-season event in the Czech Republic on 13 September, before the Grand Final in Spain on 23 September.

title: The tiny town aiming to defy odds in Bundesliga debut
description: Elversberg has no train station and a population of just 13,000, but its football team have enjoyed a meteoric rise from the regional German leagues to the Bundesliga.
fullText:
In south-west Germany, close to the border of France, lies the small town of Elversberg.

It has no railway station and a population of just 13,000, but on Saturday it will enjoy a moment of history as its football team plays in the Bundesliga for the first time.

The club have enjoyed a meteoric rise, having gone from the regional leagues in Germany to the top flight in just a few years.

And their coach Vincent Wagner has not played down the enormity of the task ahead for his side.

"For the team to avoid relegation in the top flight would be like a journey to Mars," he said.

But Elversberg are well-versed in defying the odds, and will aim to do so again this season.

"It might sound like the rise has been a rush but at every stage the floor was solid before the next one was built," Elversberg's technical director Josef Welzmuller said.

"We did it step by step and it didn't feel like a fairytale for the people here because they are so strong in their decision-making and very clear in how they want to play and we want to act as a club.

"This is the whole magic to be honest, and a lot of very, very hard work."

With three promotions in the past five years, Elversberg have swiftly climbed from the fourth tier of German football to the top flight.

It is not unusual in football for a small team to enjoy a rapid rise - Wrexham have famously done just that having gone from non-league football to the Championship.

But while they have been helped by having wealthy owners, Elversberg have never had similar financial clout - and as a result have had to do things a little differently.

A key figure in Elversberg being able to rise as quickly as they have was Ole Book.

A former footballer in Germany's lower leagues, Book joined Elversberg in 2017 as a scout, and within a year was promoted to sporting director.

Book had an eye for spotting talented youngsters and giving them the platform to showcase their emerging talent by becoming key players in the Elversberg team.

One of those players was Nick Woltemade, who was brought in on loan from Werder Bremen II in 2022 and went on to score 10 goals that season. Woltemade then joined Stuttgart before his £69m club record move to Newcastle last year.

Book's impressive work at Elversberg ultimately caught the eye of Borussia Dortmund, who appointed him as sporting director in April, with the club specifically highlighting his ability to find and develop young players, "creating value for the squad".

Despite his departure, Elversberg have not changed their philosophy for the coming campaign, with talented youth being the main focus of their recruitment.

"We won't do anything different," Welzmuller added.

"The identity stays the same and it is built on three core pillars. The first is to be brave, the second is to be intense and the third is to be clever.

"You will see when you watch us we want high-intensity players, and that will stay the same forever."

A difficult season lies ahead, with Elversberg having to face the likes of Harry Kane's Bayern Munich, Bayer Leverkusen and Dortmund.

The fans and residents of the town are excited by the challenge, and the club are represented everywhere when you walk through the streets.

"What happened in the last few years was exceptional for the town," Welzmuller said.

"When you walk or drive through the town at the moment you see Elversberg flags all around and you see people walking around with the team's merchandise like a hat or jersey, which makes us all feel very proud.

"I feel like the club is part of the life of the people here."

First to visit the town are Leverkusen - the team that produced their own fairytale just two years ago by winning the Bundesliga title unbeaten.

"For us, the Bundesliga feels so far away at times. And yet, if you set aside the infrastructure and the money and just focus on playing football, we can - funnily enough - somehow already keep up with the pace," he said.

"We've had a long and intensive pre-season, strengthened the team as much as we could, and managed to keep most of the players we wanted to keep.

"The team is ready for the Bundesliga."

title: GB's Fery into first ATP Tour final as opponent retires
description: Arthur Fery is into his first ATP Tour final as opponent James Duckworth retires because of injury at the Winston-Salem Open.
fullText:
Britain's Arthur Fery has reached his first ATP Tour final after opponent James Duckworth retired because of injury at the Winston-Salem Open.

The 24-year-old was leading 6-4 2-1 in the semi-final when his Australian opponent, who called for a medical timeout after the first set, forfeited the match.

Fery is the first Briton to reach the final of the ATP 250 event and his progress continues after his surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.

He has also reached a career high of 33 in the world and overtaken Cameron Norrie to become British number one.

"I am really happy to be in the final," said Fery.

"Not the way I wanted it to end at all. I hope James will get well soon and rest up for next week. But I am very happy to be through."

Fery faces Ignacio Buse in Saturday's final in North Carolina after the 22-year-old beat France's Benjamin Bonzi 6-2 4-6 6-1.

Peru's Buse, who is ranked 36th in the world, will be aiming to win his second title of the season after beating Tommy Paul at the ATP 500 event in Hamburg in May.

Only eight weeks ago, before Fery's remarkable run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, he was ranked outside the top 100.

His maiden ATP final appearance against Buse comes before next month's US Open, where he just missed out on being seeded.

Fery has been drawn against Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti in the opening round at Flushing Meadows in New York.

title: Slow start makes me want to stay - Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030
description: In an exclusive BBC Sport interview, Lando Norris explains why he has signed a new contract that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.
fullText:
Lando Norris says signing a new contract that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030 was "quite an easy yes for me".

The world champion, whose new deal was announced on Saturday, said he "didn't even have a look" at other teams before deciding to commit his future to the team he has been with since his Formula 1 debut in 2019.

"There was some interest from elsewhere," Norris said in an interview with BBC Sport, "but I don't want to go anywhere. I don't want to be with another team. I don't want to spend time with other people.

"That's why it really was probably one of the easiest decisions I've made since being in Formula 1."

The Briton had no need to rush his decision to commit to McLaren because his existing contract still had more than a year to run.

But he says the idea "became a topic of conversation over the last four months or so, but very loosely in the background" and he had no hesitation in agreeing.

Norris says his loyalty to McLaren is based on the relationships he has within the team - starting with chief executive officer Zak Brown and team principal Andrea Stella - and their shared history.

After Norris made his F1 debut in 2019, they spent several years struggling for competitiveness, before their form turned around quickly after Stella was promoted at the end of 2022.

The team won consecutive constructors' championships in 2024 and 2025 - ending a drought that went back to 1998 - and the drivers' title for Norris last year.

The 26-year-old said: "The fact I stuck it through with them and then we went on to obviously have success certainly makes me feel like I don't want to... they didn't give up on me and I didn't give up on them.

"That just creates a very strong bond between everyone that works here. I want to believe that bond stays as strong as it is now 'til I do retire in my career at Formula 1.

"I know that's a long, long way away and I don't want to think of it. But I believe we're in the best place we've ever been even with a tough start to the season. And I believe that we can fight through anything together for sure."

McLaren started this season well off the pace they had shown through 2024 and 2025 as they struggled to get on top of the new rules introduced to F1 this year.

But Norris says that only made him want to stay at the team more.

"That's exactly the situation that doesn't take me away from where I am or doesn't influence anything else," he said.

"I still have had a lot of fun and enjoy working and trying to fight through the tougher moments with the people that I do it with now. I don't want to fight through moments with anyone else.

"This beginning of the year is the perfect example of what doesn't make me turn my head the other way or anything.

"In fact, it's more the opposite. It makes me want to stick with the people that I am with because I believe we can fight back through most circumstances and all circumstances. And I enjoy the fight in some ways just as much as I enjoy the experience of being on top."

He added: "People get too hung up sometimes on saying, 'is it the right place?' I believe it is, but even if it wasn't, the fact that I can just say I'm a driver for McLaren and I race for McLaren, that makes me happy enough."

McLaren have improved their performance significantly in recent races. After a major upgrade to their car, Norris has won the past two grands prix, in Hungary and the Netherlands.

That has reduced the gap between him and Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli to 83 points with 11 races remaining - although the war in the Middle East may affect the number of races that end up being staged.

Norris said before the British Grand Prix in July that he had been frustrated at not being able to defend his title.

Now, he says: "I'm starting the fight of defending it. I'm trying to. I'm doing my best. We all are. As a team, we're doing our best. They want to allow me to fight for it and of course I just want to fight for it. So, it's a big challenge.

"It's still a big mountain to climb in terms of trying to achieve it. But for a while now, we've been very, very close to being in the position that we are now, where we can fight for wins and podiums and we can fight the people we need to fight against.

"So, I'm certainly more confident than I have been, especially the first part of the year.

"But it still just takes a lot of work and there's a lot of things we need to improve on but we're confident as a team that we can try to achieve it."

Team principal Andrea Stella said: "Lando is an exceptional driver, who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren but, above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team.

"Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1.

"This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.

"With him and Oscar [Piastri, Norris' team-mate], we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1."

Zak Brown, chief executive officer of McLaren Racing, said: "Lando's journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves."

title: Cannabis smell at US Open is distracting - Boulter
description: British number one Katie Boulter complains that the smell of cannabis is putting her off her game at the US Open.
fullText:
British number one Katie Boulter has complained that the smell of cannabis is putting her off her game at the US Open.

On Sunday, the final major of the season begins at Flushing Meadows in New York, where cannabis is legal for adults aged 21 and over.

Though smoking is not permitted on site, the smell of cannabis wafts on to court from nearby Corona Park and has bothered a number of players in previous years, including Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev.

Boulter, who is preparing to face American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee in the first round, says it is possible to smell cannabis "a lot" on the practice courts.

"I'm not a huge fan of it," said Boulter, the world number 60. "I know a lot of players have complained on some of the specific courts. I've played on one before and I did smell it during my match.

"It's something that I wouldn't like to smell in the middle of my match. I'm trying to focus and then obviously, it takes you out of the moment and you really don't want to.

"You don't need distractions. So yeah, I wasn't a huge fan of it."

The smell of cannabis has been a persistent issue at the US Open.

In 2022, Australian Open doubles champion Nick Kyrgios complained that a fan was triggering his asthma by smoking courtside, prompting the umpire to ask supporters to refrain.

Greece's Maria Sakkari pointed the smell out to an umpire midway through a set in 2023, later clarifying that it wasn't an excuse for her defeat.

The United States Tennis Association, which organises the event, says it works with the local police and parks department to reduce smoking on the site boundary.

It said: "While we can't control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this."

Britain's Fran Jones and Harriet Dart, who both qualified on Friday, have also noticed the smell.

"Last year I made a joke about that, in my first round, and I said to the guy, 'is this normal?'" said Jones, whose tournament begins against Poland's Magda Linette on Monday.

"Because I was on the stadium, and it's next to the park. He's like, 'yeah". and I was like: 'Well, no wonder I'm playing pretty well.'

"This year I'll be like 'no, lock in, lock in!'"

After beating British compatriot Heather Watson in qualifying to set up a first-round match against the United States' Peyton Stearns, Dart said: "I mean it's New York. It's New York.

"I feel like everywhere you walk around, it's everywhere, no?

"It is what it is. Same for everyone."

title: Liverpool agree £123m deal for PSG's Barcola
description: Liverpool are closing in on a deal to sign forward Bradley Barcola, which will increase doubts over Cody Gakpo's future.
fullText:
Liverpool have agreed a deal worth up to £123m for Paris St-Germain forward Bradley Barcola.

PSG initially valued the France attacker at £145m, but the Reds have agreed a package worth an initial £106m with £17m in potential add-ons.

The 23-year-old is expected to have a medical this weekend before signing a long-term contract at Anfield.

Right-footed Barcola prefers to play on the left wing and his impending arrival will increase the doubts around Cody Gakpo's future at Liverpool.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport both Tottenham Hotspur and Manchester City have shown interest in the Netherlands forward.

Liverpool are also in the market for a right winger, having explored moves for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh and Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr.

Barcola has become a main target for Liverpool as they look to bolster their attack following the departures of Luis Diaz and Mohamed Salah in the past two summers.

He moved to PSG from Lyon in 2023 for a reported £38.5m and has won three Ligue 1 titles, two Champions Leagues, the French Cup twice, as well as the Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Intercontinental Cup.

Barcola, who scored three goals for France in this summer's World Cup, can also play on the right or through the middle and could provide cover for Alexander Isak while Hugo Ekitike recovers from a serious Achilles injury.

Speaking before Saturday's game against Nottingham Forest (12:30 BST), Reds boss Andoni Iraola was asked about Gakpo's future and said he "cannot guarantee anything", but wants to keep the 27-year-old at the club.

"[Gakpo] has been very good since he came back from the World Cup and his holiday, with a very good attitude. I hope we can keep him at that level because I think he has been very influential in our games," Iraola he said.

The strengths Barcola will bring to Anfield

Barcola has been a priority for Liverpool since Yan Diomande opted to join Real Madrid earlier in the window. The Frenchman's move to Anfield - for up to £123m - would be a record fee for a player leaving Ligue 1.

Barcola will bring star factor and inject real quality into a Liverpool attack that could become feared if last summer's expensive signings Isak and Florian Wirtz can step up.

PSG can feasibly look at the deal as an excellent outcome, given they signed Barcola for £38m and will more than triple their money - if add-ons are met - for a player who is entering the last two years of his contract and has shown no willingness to sign an extension.

Barcola was often behind Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the wings in the biggest games last season and PSG have added to their options in those areas this summer by signing Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts.

However Liverpool will be pleased with the deal too, having held firm earlier in the summer in terms of meeting PSG's valuation of £145m - but eventually bringing in one of Europe's most exciting forwards.

title: Lampard 'somewhere in the middle' of Mourinho and Ancelotti
description: Eight years into his own managerial career, Coventry City boss Frank Lampard cites Jose Mourinho and Carli Ancelotti as the main influences on his style.
fullText:
The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

In the second episode of the new season, available on Saturday, 29 August, musician Tom Grennan sits down with Coventry City manager Frank Lampard.

As a player, Frank Lampard worked under some of the biggest managers in the game, including Jose Mourinho, Carlo Ancelotti, Guus Hiddink and Rafael Benitez - not to mention his uncle Harry Redknapp.

Eight years into his own managerial career, the Coventry City boss cited Mourinho and Ancelotti as the main influences on his style.

"Jose and Carlo are like both sides of the coin," the 48-year-old told BBC Sport.

"Jose was very on you, he transmitted his self-confidence, but if you stepped out of line or did something wrong, you'd feel the strength of him, whereas Carlo was chilled and calm. When you look back, you go, 'that's a nice environment to work in'. It felt like he trusted you. So I try and take little snippets. I'm probably somewhere in the middle."

Lampard played under Mourinho and Ancelotti at Chelsea and won the Premier League and FA Cup with them both.

He said it is important to strike a balance between the pair as he targets more success with Coventry.

"I start to sometimes go towards being Jose, sometimes I go and be a bit more Carlo," he added.

"I've learnt that young managers, you come in and feel like you have to to criticise a bad performance or say something about an individual that turns up late. The more I've done this job, I realise that they're all humans.

"Sometimes a lad comes in late, you don't know the back story. And so trying to jump on him and being this hard man manager, you've got to be more Carlo. But then if you're a bit more relaxed sometimes and people are on the pitch, not doing their job, sometimes you've got a bit more Jose."

Lampard said he is not driven by trying to convince the sceptics after leading Coventry back to the Premier League for the first time in 25 years.

"The thing about modern-day football – you're brilliant one minute, you might not be brilliant the next and then everyone will let you know that," he told musician and Sky Blues fan Tom Grennan.

"You've got to be careful trying to prove every doubter wrong, because it's not possible."

Lampard guided Coventry to win the Championship with 95 points last season after taking over at the club in November 2024.

Prior to that, his managerial experience could be described as a mixed bag. After taking over at Derby in 2018, the former Chelsea midfielder led them to the Championship play-off final, where they lost to Aston Villa.

Following that, he had abortive spells in the Premier League with Chelsea and Everton, lasting 18 months at Stamford Bridge before being sacked in January 2021, and lasting less than a year at Goodison Park before being sacked in January 2023.

"My personal ambition to prove any doubters wrong is sort of always there, but I try not to let that be my driver," Lampard explained.

"I've been in the Premier League as a player, I've been as a manager, I understand the challenge of it. I can't get ahead of myself and I can't worry too much about the outside world because otherwise you succumb to it, you'd be making different decisions."

As a player, Lampard won three Premier League titles and the Champions League in 2012. He also won four FA Cups, two League Cups and the Europa League.

He described last season's promotion with Coventry as being on par with some of those achievements.

"When you get promoted, it's hard to balance against winning the Champions League with Chelsea," Lampard said.

"Winning in Munich was the best footballing night of my life as a player by far. But then when you do something with a club that's been through what it's been through, when you work with a group of lads that are so great as a dressing room - I've never experienced, especially as a coach, to have such a good group.

"When we got promoted against Blackburn, I had a rush of pure emotion, it all came on top of me. It certainly goes right up there in things I've managed to achieve."

Lampard said that his side will have to adapt to the different challenge this season after entering the top flight, especially defensively.

"We want to keep hold of the good things from last year," he added.

"We'd be fools to think that we'd just go and play like we did in the 'Champ' every week when we dominated a lot of games."

In terms of ambitions for the season, he wants his players to be brave.

"Everyone's going to ask me, 'staying in the league, is that your target?'," Lampard said.

"Of course it would be success, because it's such a big challenge for us, but in the beginning, we'll go into it and go, 'let's stick our chests out and let's be brave about it'.

"These boys have earned where they've got to, so go in with that attitude. There's a lot to lose, but go and show yourselves."

Coventry lost 3-0 to champions Arsenal in the opening match of the season. They will host fellow promoted side Hull City on Saturday, in their first home game of the campaign.

title: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres
description:
Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy
Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”.
The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy

Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”.

The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”.

The Greens’ call for a pause comes amid one of the UK’s worst droughts in years and predictions that datacentres’ electricity use, now standing at about 2.5% of the UK’s supply, will rise fourfold by 2030.

Datacentres contain the processing chips that power billions of AI prompts every day and Labour has designated them as critical national infrastructure, a decision Polanski called “outrageous”. “To most people critical infrastructure means hospitals, water, electricity,” he said. “It doesn’t mean artificial intelligence.”

He added: “Right now the government is putting our communities, our water security and our climate ambitions second to the demands of tech giants.”

A spokesperson for the government said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data.”

They said critical national infrastructure status did not give datacentres priority access to water or electricity, nor did it automatically put them ahead of households during shortages, and that in England datacentres’ water usage represented less than 1% of non-household water consumption.

The row comes amid increasing signs that datacentre policy, already a major political issue in the US midterm elections, is rising up the agenda in Britain. In energy- and water-rich Scotland, the Scottish National party government appears to be “inching towards a moratorium” amid voter pressure, while local disputes have erupted from Devon to Buckinghamshire and Cardiff to Fife where residents have raised fears about noise, heat, traffic and the visual impact of datacentres affecting house prices.

The AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has linked the need for more AI datacentres to strong defence and this month claimed the British public “doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity.”

The government spokesperson said its refusal to pause development “does not mean a blank cheque for big tech or that every datacentre should be approved”. They said developers should “prioritise clean power, use water responsibly, create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built”.

The tech equity campaign group Foxglove warned that with some datacentre developers seeking to mitigate long waits to connect to the energy grid by planning their own gas-fired power stations, there was a risk of a “deeply alarming backward step on climate action”.

Rosa Curling, its co-executive director, said: “It’s good to hear that the government thinks there shouldn’t be a ‘blank cheque’ for big tech’s datacentres. But without urgent action, that’s exactly what will happen – the public and the planet will be left to foot the bill for the environmental and social costs of these energy-hungry giants.”

title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
description: Her family is among hundreds anxiously waiting for news after the deadly flash floods.
fullText:
Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.

She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.

Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.

But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.

"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.

The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.

She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.

"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."

The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.

She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.

She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.

A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.

There was little to suggest what was coming.

"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."

The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.

After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.

Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.

"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."

At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.

He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.

The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.

"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.

"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."

Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.

They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.

Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.

Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."

Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.

"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."

She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.

The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.

Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."

For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.

Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.

Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list of 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.

For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

title: Autopsy shows Tennessee National Guard fatally shot 20-year-old armed man in the back
description: Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press sh...
fullText:
Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press shows, contradicting police accounts that the man was facing the troops when they fired.

Authorities have said Tyrin Johnson turned toward guard members with a gun while running from them in the early morning hours after the Fourth of July holiday when he was fatally shot in the chest.

But according to an autopsy report shared Thursday by Johnson's family, a single bullet went in the right side of his back and exited through his upper right chest. The autopsy findings, reported earlier by The Commercial Appeal newspaper, were prepared by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center Office of the Medical Examiner, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The guard members were assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democratic-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

Johnson's grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said guard members had no justification to shoot his grandson in the back.

"If he ain't caused you no threat, you know what I'm saying, you have no reason to be killing," said the former correctional officer with the Davidson County Sheriff's Office in Nashville.

Officers responded to a call of shots fired a few blocks from Beale Street and saw a person armed with a gun leaving, said Memphis police. Two Guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who "rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them," according to a Tennessee National Guard report obtained by the Associated Press. Both troops fired their service weapons, M17 handguns, and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the guard report said.

The bullet had a slightly upward trajectory through Tyrin Johnson's body, the autopsy report said. That would be consistent with him running away from the shooter, said Dr. Steven White, a certified forensic pathologist who did not do Johnson's autopsy but reviewed the report for the AP.

The report said there was no soot, gunpowder stippling or muzzle imprint around the wound, which White said indicated Johnson was likely shot from more than 3 feet away.

"Be transparent – you shot him in the back," Evaniel Johnson added. "I just want to make sure somebody be responsible for what happened. Some accountability. They ain't never going to bring my grandson back."

In the autopsy report, an "investigative narrative" based on an account from an agent with the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation also stated Tyrin Johnson was turning toward law enforcement with a gun.

"The unknown male grabbed at his waistband," the report stated. "Law enforcement officers saw the unknown male draw a firearm. Law enforcement officers then shot at the unknown male, striking him once in the chest."

Andre Wharton, an attorney representing Johnson's family, told the AP that the narrative presented by law enforcement does not match the autopsy findings of a single bullet wound in the back.

"I just see some kind of blatant inconsistency there, in terms of what law enforcement reports," Wharton said. "The versions don't seem to match."

The manner of death is listed as "homicide," which typically is used when a death is caused by the actions of another person but often doesn't factor in intent or carry any legal weight. To date, no criminal charges have been filed.

TBI said the investigation is "open and ongoing" and directed AP to the medical examiner's office when asked to confirm the autopsy findings. The AP has a pending request for a copy for Johnson's autopsy from the Shelby County Medical Examiner's office.

Johnson was carrying a "handgun magazine with rounds," according to the autopsy report. Wharton said it was not illegal for Johnson to be carrying the ammunition in Tennessee.

Johnson's family has asked authorities to show them surveillance video or other evidence he was pointing a weapon at guard members. The family has still not been shown any video of the moments leading up to the shooting, Evaniel Johnson said.

Trump's decision to send Tennessee National Guard troops to Memphis to combat crime was met with a mixed response from residents and was the subject of a lawsuit, though it did not result in widespread protests.

title: Trump has his eye on these Pacific island nations
description: Trump's latest Truth Social post labels two Pacific island nations as U.S. territories, fueling fresh questions about his expansion ambitions.
fullText:
A new Truth Social post from President Donald Trump is raising eyebrows after it appeared to portray two Pacific island nations as U.S. territories, even though both are independent countries.

The post adds Micronesia and the Marshall Islands to a growing list of places Trump has discussed bringing under U.S. ownership, control or influence.

The White House has not explained the post, but it is the latest example of Trump's interest in expanding U.S. influence beyond its current borders. Since returning to office, the president has revived calls to acquire Greenland, floated the idea of making Venezuela the 51st state and suggested the United States could one day claim control of the Strait of Hormuz.

USA TODAY contacted the White House for comment but had not received a response as of Aug. 28.

More: 'Lake America'? Trump's Canada snub prompts backlash – from Americans

The Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia may be independent countries, but both have deep historical ties to the United States.

After World War II, the United States administered both island nations as part of a U.N.-backed trust territory in the Pacific. The Marshall Islands gained independence in 1979, while Micronesia became independent in 1990.

Even after independence, the countries maintained close ties with Washington through what's known as a Compact of Free Association, or COFA.

Under the agreements, the United States provides financial assistance and access to certain federal services, while retaining key defense and security responsibilities in the region.

According to the Department of the Interior, the compacts give residents of the Marshall Islands and Micronesia access to programs and services that include the U.S. Postal Service and National Weather Service. The agreements have also made the islands important U.S. partners in a strategically significant part of the Pacific.

Those longstanding ties help explain why the two nations are often closely associated with the United States, even though they are sovereign countries rather than U.S. territories.

The Marshall Islands and Micronesia are not the first places to become wrapped up in Trump's comments about expanding U.S. territory.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has repeatedly argued that Greenland, the autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic, is critical to U.S. national security. The president first floated the idea of purchasing Greenland during his first term before reviving the proposal after his reelection.

"We need Greenland for national security," Trump said in December. "You look up and down the coast, you have Russian and Chinese ships all over the place. We need it for national security. We have to have it."

Trump has also turned his attention to Venezuela. Earlier this year, he said he had seriously considered making the oil-rich South American nation the 51st U.S. state. The idea gained renewed attention following a U.S. military operation that led to the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.

The president has since suggested the United States could temporarily oversee Venezuela and its oil infrastructure, adding the country to a growing list of territories and strategic locations Trump has discussed bringing under greater U.S. control.

With Micronesia and the Marshall Islands now appearing in a post labeled "U.S. Territories," Trump's latest social media message is fueling fresh questions about how far those ambitions extend.

USA TODAY's Joey Garrison and Reuters contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Trump has his eye on these Pacific island nations
